newsitem.title: FRANCE: Floating museum will honour French-US ties.
newsitem.headline: Floating museum will honour French-US ties.

text.p: Thousands flocked to the French Atlantic port of Rochefort this weekend to watch the ceremonial laying of the keel of a sailship identical to the one which took the Marquis de Lafayette to the aid of American revolutionaries over 200 years ago.

The colours of the United States and France flew in the streets of the graceful seaside city throughout the weekend, beginning with the main ceremony in Rochefort's historical shipyard on Friday evening, America's July 4 Independence Day.

The vessel, the frigate Hermione, named after its ancestor which sailed in 1780 to the aid of American revolutionaries fighting for independence from Britain, is to be a floating museum to Franco-American friendship and to the ancient art of sailship building, site director Emmanuel de Fontaignieu said.
The three-masted, 44-metre-long sailing vessel will take up to 10 years to build and will sail to Boston once launched before returning to Rochefort.

The ship is being built in the same shipyard where the original Hermione was built in 1779. The building site is open to visitors from this weekend and is expected to draw some 20,000 tourists this summer, Fontaignieu told Reuters.

A smilar project in the Netherlands, that of the construction site of the vessel Batavia, has proved to be one of that country's most popular new tourist attractions, regularly drawing thousands of visitors eager to watch the ship being built.

The Hermione construction is expected to cost around 50 million francs (more than $8 million), said Benedict Donnelly, Franco-American head of the Hermione-Lafayette Association which initiated the project. Financing is both public and private.
"This would have been an entirely happy occasion but it is marred by the absence of the former U.S. ambassador to France Pamela Harriman who, as you know, died suddenly late last year," he said.

"She was one of our main supporters throughout and agreed with us that Lafayette was the very symbol of Franco-American friendship and that his memory should be honoured throughout the ages," Donnelly said.

Gilbert Mortier, Marquis de Lafayette was only a teenager when he offered his services to George Washington, the American revolutionary leader and later first president of the United States, shortly after the revolution's start in 1776.
Lafayette had defied then-King Louis XVI who wanted to stay out of the conflict.
But his notable role in the war changed royal opinion and he returned to France in 1779 to campaign for French intervention.
He was successful and returned to the United States aged 21.
In 1780 he boarded the Hermione to inform Washington that a French expeditionary force was being sent to his aid.

That force, together with Washington's troops, defeated the British at Yorktown while French naval forces, including the Hermione, were victorious in nearby Chesapeake Bay. The twin battles led to American independence.
Lafayette later joined the 1789 French Revolution, becoming one of its main military figures against his own class, but was soon out of favour with ultra-radicals and had to flee France.
He long lived in exile but helped King Louis-Philippe take the throne in 1830.

Lafayette's name has however mostly remained associated with Franco-American relations. American General John Pershing, arriving in France in 1917, with the American forces whose aid was a main reason for the allied victory over Germany in World War One, is reported to have said on landing: "Lafayette, we are here."
